articles.title: A British woman used more than £1 million of her elderly mother's money for holidays, cars, shopping and a lavish wedding; High Court ordered her to hand back £2.6 million after a bitter inheritance battle
articles.summary: A British woman who used more than £1 million of her elderly mother's money to fund holidays, luxury shopping, cars and family weddings has been ordered
articles.body: A British woman who used more than £1 million of her elderly mother's money to fund holidays, luxury shopping, cars and family weddings has been ordered to return the money, along with three properties worth approximately £1.6 million, following a bitter inheritance dispute with her brother. Sandra Thomas, 65, and her husband, Philip Thomas, were found to have used Jeanne MacDougall's bank accounts as their own while managing her finances under a lasting power of attorney. The High Court ruled that the couple had breached their legal responsibilities and unduly influenced Jeanne into transferring properties to them. However, the judge also upheld Jeanne's final will, which largely favoured her daughter and son-in-law.Couple spent mother's fortune on holidays, cars and lavish weddingsAccording to the court proceedings, Sandra and Philip used Jeanne's money to pay for a range of personal and family expenses, including holidays, new cars, shopping trips and meals at the prestigious London restaurant The Ivy.The spending also included their daughter's wedding at the five-star Savoy hotel, another family wedding, college fees for their children and numerous cash withdrawals.The judge, Nicola Rushton KC, said the total amount spent through Jeanne's accounts exceeded £1 million, although she did not calculate the precise figure. She noted a pattern in which properties were sold, the proceeds deposited into Jeanne's bank accounts and the money subsequently used to meet the couple's expenses."There was a clear cycle of emptying Jeanne’s bank accounts, realising an asset to generate more cash, and then repeating the process again," the judge said.She added that the couple had given no thought to how Jeanne's future care would be funded and that she had virtually no cash left when she died in 2020.Three properties worth £1.6 million transferred to coupleThe financial dispute also involved three properties that Sandra and Philip had obtained from Jeanne during her lifetime.These included a holiday home in Peacehaven, East Sussex, valued at approximately £400,000, and two flats in Ealing, west London, worth around £1.2 million combined.The judge found that the transfers resulted from undue influence by the couple over Jeanne.In the case of the Peacehaven property, the court heard that Sandra and Philip had justified the transfer by suggesting that Gary already had a holiday home in Cyprus and had received enough from the family business.However, the judge concluded that these arguments were likely used by the couple to persuade Jeanne to transfer the property.She said the transaction marked the beginning of a pattern in which decisions increasingly favoured Sandra, Philip and their family over Gary and his family.The same finding of undue influence applied to the transfers of the two Ealing flats.Brother challenged mother's final will over dementia concernsThe inheritance dispute was brought by Jeanne's son, Gary MacDougall, 70, who argued that his mother had not been mentally capable of making her final will in 2011.He claimed that Jeanne, who suffered from Alzheimer's disease, had lost much of her independence and did not properly understand the consequences of changing her will.Gary also argued that his parents had always intended their two children to receive broadly equal financial treatment and inheritance.Under Jeanne's 2008 will, properties in Avenue Crescent and Berrymead Gardens were allocated to Gary and his family, while Sandra and Philip were to receive properties in Stuart Road and Avenue Gardens. Sandra was also entitled to most of the money in Jeanne's bank accounts.However, a revised will made in 2011 left all four properties to Sandra and Philip, while Sandra continued to receive the majority of her mother's savings. Gary and Sandra were to share the remaining estate.Gary challenged the revised arrangement, arguing that his mother had been suffering from dementia when she signed the document and that her decision did not reflect the family's earlier understanding.Judge upheld will despite finding financial misconductIn a significant part of the ruling, Judge Rushton rejected Gary's challenge to the 2011 will, concluding that Jeanne had the necessary mental capacity to make it and had not been unduly influenced into changing its terms.The judge acknowledged that Jeanne was genuinely grateful to Sandra and Philip for providing her with a home and supporting her in her later years. She said it was understandable that Jeanne wanted to reward them.However, this did not excuse the couple's conduct in managing her finances.Sandra and Philip's barrister, Alexander Learmonth KC, had accepted that they overstepped their responsibilities under the lasting power of attorney by spending Jeanne's money on themselves and their family.Their defence was that they believed the spending was effectively an advance on their inheritance, as Sandra was already expected to receive most of her mother's cash under both wills. They also argued that they believed they were acting in accordance with Jeanne's wishes and had not received proper advice about their responsibilities.The judge rejected these explanations, stating that ignorance of their duties was not a defence. She described the misconduct as deliberate and driven by greed.Couple ordered to restore money and properties to mother's estateFollowing the ruling, Sandra and Philip were required to return the three properties or their value to Jeanne's estate and account for the money they had spent from her bank accounts.The three properties were worth approximately £1.6 million, while the money spent through the accounts exceeded £1 million, bringing the combined amount involved to around £2.6 million.The exact amount of compensation payable for the money taken was still to be calculated through a further accounting process.The recovered assets and compensation will increase the value of the estate's remaining assets, half of which will go to Gary under the terms of the upheld will.Despite the ruling, Sandra and Philip are still expected to receive a substantial inheritance under the 2011 will. The judge's decision therefore preserved Jeanne's final testamentary wishes while requiring the couple to restore assets that had been improperly obtained or spent during her lifetime.You use AI every day. articles.title: The festive fallout: When family togetherness turns toxic
articles.summary: In Surita Mishra’s life there is a particular kind of exhaustion that has set in after Diwali.
articles.body: In Surita Mishra’s life there is a particular kind of exhaustion that has set in after Diwali. The guests have left, the house is finally quiet, the elaborate meals have been cleared away and the photographs of smiling faces have found their way to social media. Yet, instead of feeling happy and refreshed, she and her husband are feeling strangely low, irritable or emotionally drained.They replay conversations in their heads, remember an unnecessary remark made by a relative, feel guilty about an argument or wonder why spending a few days with people they love has left them so exhausted. Even angry.For some, the relief of returning to their own homes and routines is greater than the sadness of saying goodbye.Clinical psychologist Muskaan Trikha, Institute of Neurosciences, Medanta, says, “Family gatherings bring back emotional patterns that most of us have outgrown in our lives. Returning to the same family environment of our childhood can reactivate these feelings, making old rivalries and insecurities resurface.”Growing up, we all develop a sense of identity within the family based on how we are treated, compared or recognised. When siblings are repeatedly compared in terms of academic achievements, careers, relationships or parental attention, these experiences influence how they perceive themselves and each other even in adulthood. And perceived favouritism, unequal treatment and unresolved conflicts can contribute to sibling resentment, which have a way of surfacing during festive times, adds Ms Trikha.Festivals are ideally supposed to bring families together. However, research globally over the years has shown that togetherness does not always translate into harmony. In fact, occasions that demand prolonged family interaction have more chances of exposing tensions that ordinary life, geographical distance and busy schedules help keep under control.A sibling rivalry that has remained dormant for months can suddenly surface over something as trivial as who received more attention from the parents. A seemingly innocent question about marriage, children, career or money, can reopen insecurities that have taken years to manage. Couples who generally get along well may find themselves arguing over whose family gets priority, who is expected to adjust and who has to shoulder the responsibility of keeping everyone happy.Research by sociologist Jill Suitor at Purdue University, through the ‘Within-Family Differences Study’—which followed more than 550 multigenerational families over two decades—found that disagreements over strongly held values, particularly political and religious beliefs, were an important source of family conflict. The research also highlighted how disagreements over a child’s choice of partner can strain relationships between parents and their adult children, sometimes leading to fewer visits and less frequent communication.Family members may share a surname, history and traditions, but that does not mean they share the same beliefs or values. Differences that remain manageable during the rest of the year can become difficult to navigate when everyone is expected to spend several days together. Gender roles, parenting and even food habits can become sources of friction, particularly when older and younger generations have very different ideas about how people should live.The return of old family rolesOne of the more curious aspects of family gatherings is how quickly adults can slip back into the roles they occupied as children. Dr Samant Darshi, consultant, Psychiatrist at Yatharth Super Speciality Hospital, Greater Noida, explains why: “Family gatherings often reactivate emotions and experiences associated with childhood. Even as adults, people may unconsciously return to familiar family roles, such as the responsible child, the achiever or the one who always makes compromises. These comparisons between siblings and differences in parental attention bring back feelings of inadequacy.”And now that the children are adults, coupled with the fact that we live in times when our emotional filters have vanished and family time has added to our stress — it’s like a dam burst somewhere. That’s how ugly a situation can get.As adults, we have all built independent lives, made important professional decisions and become entirely self-sufficient; hence being treated like an irresponsible teenager the moment we return to our parental home or when parents and siblings visit ours — becomes a powder-keg situation. The daughter who was always considered difficult may still be seen that way, while the son who was the family favourite may continue to receive a degree of indulgence that his siblings find difficult to accept.Returning home almost always activates these old patterns because gatherings are always about discussing shared history, childhood anecdotes. For instance, a parent may continue to offer unsolicited advice to an adult child, while the child, despite being perfectly capable of making independent decisions, reacts with the same irritation or defensiveness they experienced growing up. The exchange can quickly become less about the immediate disagreement and more about years of accumulated frustration.Sibling relationships can be equally complicated. Adulthood does not necessarily erase childhood competition, particularly when comparisons continue within the family. Who is more successful, who earns more, whose children are doing better, who spends more time with the parents and who contributes more to family responsibilities can all become sources of tension. Even when nobody explicitly raises these questions, people may carry an awareness of where they stand in the family hierarchy.Disproportionate pressure on womenThe workload behind these celebrations is another important part of the problem. Shopping, cooking, cleaning, organizing and managing needs and expectations require considerable effort. This work often falls disproportionately on women, who may find themselves responsible for ensuring that everyone feels welcome and gets along. A 2006 holiday-stress survey by the Greenberg Quinlan Rosner research group, cited by Family Psychology Associates, identified women and lower-middle-income individuals as particularly vulnerable to holiday-related stress. Respondents reported fatigue, nervousness, sadness and irritability, all of which can make it harder to manage everyday disagreements.Don’t forget about expensesMoney adds another layer. Travel, gifts, entertaining relatives, preparing elaborate meals and accommodating guests can stretch household budgets. People may feel obliged to spend more than they can comfortably afford because of family expectations or the desire to maintain appearances. The financial pressure may not always be openly discussed, but it can contribute to resentment, particularly when some family members spend freely while others are left to manage the expenses.The physical and emotional exhaustion of hosting can also affect how people respond to one another. In a 2024 article, UT Southwestern Medical Center's clinical psychologist, Dr Sarah Woods, noted that strained family relationships can contribute to stress-related symptoms such as disrupted sleep, headaches and other physical complaints. When people are already tired, overworked and emotionally stretched, their tolerance for disagreements can diminish further.Festivals provide the setting for these comparisons to become more visible. When siblings who live in different cities or countries meet after a long gap, they are suddenly confronted with each other's choices, achievements and lifestyles.What begins as catching up can turn into an unspoken assessment of who has done better in life. The problem is not necessarily that families intend to hurt one another, but that old expectations often remain intact long after people have outgrown them.Those ‘harmless-harmful’ questionsThere is also the peculiar discomfort of being asked questions that seem harmless to the person asking them but deeply personal to the person answering.When are you getting married? Why haven't you had children yet? Are you still in the same job? How much are you earning? Why don't you visit more often? Such questions carry an undertone of judgement, particularly when they touch on areas where someone is already feeling vulnerable. A person dealing with infertility, a divorce, financial uncertainty, professional disappointment or loneliness may find it difficult to respond casually to something that others consider ordinary family conversation.The expectation that everyone should be cheerful and accommodating during festivals makes these encounters harder to deal with. People often suppress their irritation because they do not want to spoil the occasion, only to find that the feelings resurface later.When togetherness becomes emotional labourFamily celebrations involve considerable emotional and physical labour, much of which remains invisible. Someone has to organise the gathering, prepare the food, arrange accommodation, buy gifts, coordinate travel and make sure everyone feels included. In many households, these responsibilities continue to fall disproportionately on women, particularly mothers and daughters, even when they are also managing professional commitments and their own families. The expectation that everyone should enjoy the festivities can mean that the people doing the most work have the least opportunity to participate in them.This imbalance can become a source of resentment, especially when some family members arrive expecting to be looked after while others are expected to manage everything. A daughter visiting her parents may find herself spending most of her time in the kitchen rather than catching up with family. A working woman may be expected to take time off, travel with children, organise gifts and accommodate relatives, while her partner's contribution is treated as optional. Such arrangements may have been accepted for years, but they can become increasingly difficult to tolerate as people's lives and expectations change.The wider social climate can also add to these tensions. The American Psychological Association’s ‘Stress in America’ 2025 survey found that 62% of US adults considered societal division a significant source of stress. Among those affected by this stress, 60% said they had lost patience or yelled at a family member because of stress.Generational differences can make matters worse. Research highlighted by the National Communication Association, US, showed that a familiar pattern of older relatives criticizing or questioning younger family members over their habits, personalities, political beliefs and lifestyle choices. Younger people, in turn, find such comments as intrusive, judgemental or meddlesome. When several generations share a home during festivals, these differences become harder to sidestep.Couples often find themselves caught between competing family expectations. Festivals can become a test of loyalty, with each partner negotiating how much time to spend with their respective parents, whose traditions should take precedence and how to deal with relatives who overstep boundaries.A partner who remains silent when their family makes an uncomfortable remark may unintentionally leave the other feeling unsupported. Disagreements that appear to be about travel plans or festive arrangements can actually be about a deeper question: whose feelings matter more, and who is expected to keep adjusting?For some couples, these gatherings expose differences that everyday life allows them to avoid. One partner may value close family involvement, while the other prefers greater independence.Relationship therapists often point to boundaries as an important part of maintaining healthy family relationships. Being close to one's family does not mean having to accommodate every demand, answer every personal question or participate in every tradition.Yet setting boundaries can be difficult, particularly in families where saying no is interpreted as disrespect, selfishness or a lack of affection. People here simply agree to things they do not want to do to avoid confrontation, accumulating resentment in the process.The emotional hangoverThe pressure to appear happy during festivals is another stressor. Social media has added another layer to this expectation, with family photographs, elaborate meals and cheerful reunions creating an impression that everyone is enjoying an uncomplicated sense of belonging.But people dealing with strained relationships, grief, separation or loneliness find this atmosphere claustrophobic. For those who have experienced family estrangement, the celebrations bring a sharper awareness of what is missing. A person who has lost a parent may find the first festival without them particularly difficult.Someone who is separated or divorced may feel uncomfortable attending gatherings where relatives continue to ask questions about the relationship. Others may feel lonely even when surrounded by family because the emotional connection they want is simply not there.What is post-event letdown?Psychologists sometimes describe the low mood that follows a period of intense social activity as a form of post-event letdown. The transition from an unusually busy, emotionally charged period to ordinary routine can be difficult. However, when the distress follows family gatherings, it may also reflect unresolved conflict, emotional exhaustion and the effort involved in managing difficult interactions.This is why some of us are relieved when the festivities end.Adds Dr Darshi, “Feeling relieved after festivals does not mean someone dislikes their family. Prolonged social interactions can be exhausting. The end of festivities allows people to return to their routines, find their personal space and bring back that sense of independence they are used to in their daily lives. The most important thing to remember here is that we can love our families while still needing emotional distance and time for ourselves.”The idea that family is where everyone should feel most comfortable is appealing, but it is not always the reality. In the season of shimmer & shine, the human thing to do is to understand that things may not be perfect. But it’s not a permanent feeling. It’ll pass.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2007, a Connecticut family preserved flowers from a garden a father had grown with his daughter; their seeds later helped launch a community project across the state
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring story of Michaela's Garden Project, where a Connecticut family's love for gardening transformed tragedy into a community initiative, ultimately honoring Michaela Petit with the designation of her four-o'clock flower as Connecticut's Children's State Flower.
articles.body: A garden in Cheshire, Connecticut, became the starting point for a project that would spread flowers across the street. According to the Connecticut Secretary of the State, the plants were four-o’clocks, grown each year by 11-year-old Michaela Petit and her father, William. After tragedy struck their family in 2007, relatives preserved the flowers. Seeds from them later helped form Michaela’s Garden Project and the flower was eventually recognised as Connecticut’s State Children’s Flower. In July 2007, Michaela, her mother, Jennifer Hawke-Petit and her older sister, Hayley, were killed in a home invasion at their Cheshire home, according to NBC Connecticut. Michaela was just 11 years old then. The garden continued to be a symbol of the time she spent with her father, planting and tending flowers.Family members saved the four-o’clocksFollowing the incident, the four-o’clock plants were moved out of the Cheshire garden by members of her family. The plants survived and flowered successfully, producing seeds. The seeds became the initial phase for Michaela‘s Garden Project, an attempt made to motivate children to be involved in service to the community. It provided schools, volunteers and community organisations with an opportunity to honour the memory of Michaela by cultivating the same type of flowers that she planted along with her father. It helped to spread the plants and gardens all over Connecticut, as well as associate gardens with service. It offered children a chance to cooperate in working with flowers. According to the Royal Horticultural Society, the flowers are Mirabilis jalapa, a bushy, tuberous perennial from tropical America. The blossoms are very fragrant and come in colours such as pink, red, yellow and white. The name four-o’clock is derived from the time when flowers start blooming, usually in the late afternoon, at about four-o’clock.The flowers became Connecticut’s Children’s State FlowerThe project had expanded to become more than just the initial family garden project. Volunteers made sure that Michaela’s four-o’clock flowers were planted in various gardens within the state. Being associated with Michaela and the community effort to promote them, there was a suggestion to honour the flowers officially. In 2015, Connecticut designated Michaela Petit’s four-o’clock as its State Children’s Flower under Public Act 15-77.The state's official account explains that the flowers were named in her memory and originated from the plants she and her father had grown together in Cheshire. It also describes how family members transplanted the flowers after her death and how the seeds helped create the garden project. Connecticut has its own designated state flower, which is the mountain laurel. The State Children’s Flower acknowledges Michaela’s four-o’clock as well as the initiative around it. This does not mean that the mountain laurel will be substituted for another state flower.A father-daughter tradition continues in gardensThe process of transporting the flowers from a single family garden to other gardens in Connecticut started with the preservation of those flowers. Plants associated with memories of Michaela and her father were preserved as seeds in order to offer other people the chance to participate in the project and grow the flowers. Four-o’clock has remained connected to the memory of Michaela and the spirit of community effort that came from her garden. The flowers tell the tale of the involvement of children and serving their communities through gardening. articles.title: California’s Salton Sea has a new conservancy and more than $500 million committed to restoration projects as dust spreads; it still shelters more than 400 bird species on the Pacific Flyway
articles.summary: Discover how California's Salton Sea, a crucial habitat for over 400 bird species, is receiving nearly half a billion dollars in funding for restoration projects to combat environmental challenges and toxic dust exposure affecting surrounding communities.
articles.body: As stated in the Salton Sea Program, California’s Salton Sea is facing an environmental challenge that affects both wildlife and nearby communities. As water levels fall, more of the lakebed is left exposed, allowing wind to carry dust into the surrounding areas and raising concerns about air quality. The shrinking water body also faces rising salinity and declining habitat conditions, putting pressure on the fish and other wildlife that depend on it. Despite these problems, the Salton Sea remains an important habitat along the Pacific Flyway, a major north-south migration corridor along western North America.According to Audubon, more than 400 bird species rely on the sea as habitat. The existing wetlands and open water in the sea are used by both resident and migratory birds as a place to feed and rest. This makes restoration essential not only for the welfare of wildlife, but also for the communities living near the area. According to California’s Governor's Office, to date, California has made a commitment worth more than $500 million in state and federal funding for the restoration and management of the Salton Sea. In April 2026, California launched the Salton Sea Conservancy, a state agency that will operate and maintain the restoration projects the Salton Sea Management Program completes, according to the Salton Sea Program.A shrinking lake leaves more exposed lake bedThe Salton Sea, located in southeastern California, is the state’s largest lake. There has been a reduction in the volume of water due to less drainage into the lake from agricultural activities. As the water volume decreases, there is an increase in salinity and exposure of the lakebed. When there are winds blowing over the exposed land area, the particles of dust are raised up and become part of the air pollution problem in the surrounding areas.But despite all these difficulties, the Salton Sea continues to be an important stopover point on the Pacific Flyway, which runs from North to South across Western North America. According to Audubon, over 400 types of birds rely on the lake for their habitat. It becomes an important aspect of the restoration plan to conserve what little habitat is left.Restoration projects are taking shapeCalifornia established the Salton Sea Management Program in 2018 as a 10-year plan for habitat restoration and dust suppression on exposed lakebed. By April 2026, the state had secured more than $500 million in combined state and federal funding for the program, according to the Governor’s Office, as reported by the Imperial Valley Press. The funding is meant for a wide range of activities but not necessarily construction of one project. One of these projects is the Species Conservation Habitat Project. It involves ponds, berms, nests and loafing islands, together with water delivery systems to benefit the fish and birds while creating shallow water habitat on exposed lakebed. California expects that the project will cover over 9000 acres upon completion.Construction of East Pond Expansion filled with water on May 22, 2025The conservancy is designed to operate and maintain restoration projects once they are built. They are responsible for operating and maintaining those projects, coordinating with public agencies and engaging local communities. This organisation controls the land and water rights necessary for the restoration projects. The future of Salton Sea depends not only on constructing but also on managing these projects. Habitat restoration, dust separation and management of completed projects will all require constant effort. This organisation provides the State of California with such an opportunity.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The political storm over an allegedly torn photograph of late Shiv Sena founder Bal Thackeray escalated on Thursday, with hundreds of Shiv Sena
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The political storm over an allegedly torn photograph of late Shiv Sena founder Bal Thackeray escalated on Thursday, with hundreds of Shiv Sena (UBT) workers taking to the streets in Mumbai to protest against Shaina NC and demand an FIR against her.The protesters, including a large number of women, gathered outside Sena Bhavan in Dadar, the headquarters of the Uddhav Thackeray-led Shiv Sena (UBT), and raised slogans against Shaina.Several protesters were later detained by police, an official said.Heavy police deployment was seen outside the premises to prevent any untoward incident and maintain law and order.The protest came a day after Shaina found herself at the centre of an embarrassing episode during a political demonstration organised by the Eknath Shinde-led Shiv Sena against Congress leader Sonia Gandhi's remarks on Hindutva ideologue VD Savarkar in her memoir, 'Belonging: A Journey of Love'.During the protest, Shiv Sena leaders, including Shaina, tore copies and pages of the book to register their opposition to Gandhi's remarks. The Shinde-led party also sought to target the rival Sena (UBT), which is currently allied with the Congress.However, the demonstration took an unexpected turn when Shaina inadvertently tore a paper carrying a photograph of Bal Thackeray. The picture showed the Shiv Sena founder slapping an effigy of former Union minister and Congress veteran Mani Shankar Aiyar.Someone immediately pointed out the mistake to Shaina. Startled, she was seen whispering "sorry" before placing the partly torn paper back on the table.Shaina NC apologised for her actions on Thursday, saying she was sorry if they had inadvertently hurt the sentiments of genuine Shiv Sainiks or admirers of Bal Thackeray.However, the Sena leader maintained that she did not need anyone's certificate to prove her love and loyalty towards the late party supremo.The incident quickly became political ammunition for the opposition, with the Shiv Sena (UBT), Raj Thackeray's Maharashtra Navnirman Sena and Congress targeting Shaina over the episode.Shaina later took to X to defend herself, claiming that she had torn the image of Congress leader Mani Shankar Aiyar and not Bal Thackeray."Hindu Hriday Samrat, respected Balasaheb Thackeray, is a deity to us. Similarly, Veer Savarkar was a Hindu Samrat to us. Regarding that photo at the book launch where Balasaheb Thackeray is hitting Mani Shankar Aiyar with a slipper, and we are tearing Mani Shankar Aiyar's face, if anyone has taken objection upon seeing that, I apologize to them," Shaina NC said.Maharashtra deputy chief minister and Shiv Sena chief Eknath Shinde also came out in her support, dismissing the allegations and clarifying that the torn portion of the photograph showed Aiyar's face."Balasaheb is like a deity to us," Shinde said, backing his party spokesperson amid the row.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2023 Caltech scientists beamed a microwave signal from a satellite in orbit to a rooftop on Earth; the experiment demonstrated wireless power transmission from space
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking experiment in 2023, Caltech scientists successfully transmitted solar power wirelessly from a satellite in orbit to Earth, marking a significant milestone in renewable energy technology.
articles.body: For years, scientists have explored whether satellites could collect sunlight in space and send the energy wirelessly to Earth. In 2023, researchers at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) tested an important part of that area. Solar energy was harvested by their spacecraft and turned into electrical energy, which was then transferred to Earth using a microwave beam. They also had an energy receiver set up on the roof of a laboratory building in Pasadena that would receive the beam. The experiment proved that there was a way to get energy from space using a prototype, but the energy could not be used for any practical purpose.Caltech launched its solar power demonstrator in January 2023The SSPD-1 satellite, developed by Caltech, launched on January 3, 2023, on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-6 rideshare mission, according to Caltech. It was carried to orbit aboard Momentus’s Vigoride-5 orbital transfer vehicle, which hosted three experimental payloads for a future solar power station. The first payload was MAPLE (Microwave Array for Power-transfer Low-orbit Experiment). It was created by the research team led by Caltech’s professor Ali Hajimiri. The MAPLE technology transmitter operated using custom-built chips. They enabled power transfer without any mechanical movement of the elements. DOLCE was used for testing the lightweight expandable space structure. ALBA had 32 types of photovoltaic cells.MAPLE transmitted power inside the spacecraft and towards EarthAccording to Caltech, MAPLE first achieved wireless power transmission on March 3, 2023. MAPLE transmitted microwave energy to two receiving arrays situated roughly a foot apart within the craft. The energy was then transformed into direct current electricity, which powered two small light-emitting diodes. The timing of the signals from MAPLE’s transmitter made the electromagnetic waves interfere constructively, forming a beam that could be steered electronically in the desired direction.According to Caltech, receiving equipment on the roof of the Gordon and Betty Moore Laboratory of Engineering in Pasadena picked up a microwave signal from the spacecraft on May 22, 2023. The signal arrived at the expected time and frequency and the frequency shifted just as the researchers had predicted from the Doppler effect caused by the satellite’s motion in orbit. Caltech announced the result on June 1, 2023. The detected power was not enough for practical electricity generation, but it confirmed that MAPLE could transmit a signal from orbit and that researchers could detect it on the ground.Why collect solar energy in space?Solar cells on Earth need light as well as good weather conditions. In the designs Caltech envisions, a solar power system in space would not be affected by nighttime, seasons or clouds. The SSPD-1 demonstrator itself flew in low-Earth orbit, where it regularly passes through Earth’s shadow. Caltech’s future perspective is based on spacecraft that gather sunlight, convert it to electricity and send microwaves to the receiver on Earth. MAPLE experiments continued for eight months after the initial demonstrations, according to Caltech. Caltech later stated that some transmitter elements were subject to failure under stress conditions, resulting in the reduction of transmission power.In its January 16, 2024, mission report, Caltech described the mission’s successes and technical lessons. Commercial-scale solar power from space remains a future goal. The 2023 prototype was not built to generate electricity for homes or businesses, but the experiment showed that it could transmit microwave power from orbit and direct a detectable signal toward Earth.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2024, Melinda French Gates gave 12 leaders $20 million each to distribute; a November 18 report says nearly all $240 million has been given out, with 91% of grants going to groups new to Pivotal
articles.summary: In 2024, Melinda French Gates gave 12 leaders $20 million each to distribute through her philanthropic organisation Pivotal, with no strings attached
articles.body: In 2024, Melinda French Gates gave 12 leaders $20 million each to distribute through her philanthropic organisation Pivotal, with no strings attached beyond a deadline of the end of 2026. A November 18 report by The Associated Press (AP) says nearly all of the $240 million has now been given out, with 91 percent of the grants going to groups that had never received Pivotal funding before.The Global Leaders programme was part of French Gates’ broader plan to donate $1 billion to support women and girls. Its early results suggest that giving trusted figures freedom to direct large sums can reach organisations that traditional funders may overlook. Read more about it, as per the report, here:How the programme workedFrench Gates launched the Global Leaders programme in 2024 through Pivotal. She gave $20 million to each of 12 leaders, including psychologist Alfiee Breland-Noble, former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern, athlete Allyson Felix, and Afghan educator Shabana Basij-Rasikh. The only requirement was that the money be donated by the end of 2026. Beyond that, the leaders had freedom to decide which organisations or causes to support, as per AP and NPR.The programme was designed to expand who gets to make funding decisions. French Gates said the goal was to partner with experts whose firsthand knowledge could broaden Pivotal’s perspective and deepen its impact.What the money has fundedAccording to Pivotal, the average grant distributed by the Global Leaders was about $240,000. The organisation says 91 percent of the donations went to groups that had not previously received funding from Pivotal.That figure is significant because it suggests the programme reached beyond Pivotal’s usual network. Rather than concentrating money among familiar recipients, the leaders used their own knowledge and communities to identify organisations that needed support.The grants covered a wide range of issues. Some focused on mental health, others on maternal health, and others on gender equality and community support.How leaders used their fundsBreland-Noble created The MATTIE Fund to distribute her $20 million. She supported established groups such as the Asian Mental Health Collective but also sought out smaller organisations through Google, LinkedIn, Instagram, and audiences at her speaking events.Her search led her to BackSpinz Music Academy in North Carolina, which trains young people to use their creativity, and Daddy Stroller Social Club, which helps new fathers deal with postpartum depression. Breland-Noble said the opportunity allowed her to help others in the same way she had been helped.Ardern took a different approach. She used her $20 million to build new solutions rather than making large gifts to established organisations.Ardern’s focus on maternal healthArdern worked with the International Rescue Committee on a programme to prevent postpartum hemorrhaging for women in areas affected by war and other humanitarian crises. The resulting Safer Births in Crises Consortium now focuses on preventing maternal deaths in South Sudan, Burkina Faso, and Papua New Guinea.She said the work took time because she wanted to create something that might not have existed otherwise. The approach reflects a more hands on use of the funding rather than simply distributing grants.Ardern also noted that her donations coincided with cuts to international aid. She said that reality made the work more urgent and pushed her to think about how to advocate for restoring support.A model for trust based givingGary Barker, founder and CEO of the Equimundo Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, used his $20 million to expand his work and attract other funders. He launched the Caring Masculinity Fund to distribute the money.Barker said the experience changed how he approaches fundraising. He said he no longer wants to return to piecemeal fundraising and hopes to build similar relationships with other funders.The programme’s early results suggest that trust based philanthropy can work. By giving leaders freedom to direct large sums, Pivotal was able to reach organisations that might not have received funding otherwise.What comes nextPivotal says a final report on the Global Leaders programme will come next year. The organisation is already looking for ways to build on the model and encourage other donors to do the same.Haven Ley, Pivotal’s chief strategy officer, said the programme was not just about impact. He said it was also about testing a model that the organisation found intriguing.French Gates said the different vantage points on the world’s challenges made Pivotal more responsive and helped the Global Leaders be more impactful. The results so far suggest that approach may have lasting value.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An Indonesian clinic lets patients pay medical bills with tree seedlings instead of money; its unusual conservation model has now won a €250,000 award
articles.summary: What if paying a doctor's bill meant planting a tree instead of handing over money?
articles.body: What if paying a doctor's bill meant planting a tree instead of handing over money? In Indonesia's West Kalimantan province, a healthcare initiative is turning this unusual idea into a conservation effort. Run by the non-profit organisation Alam Sehat Lestari (ASRI), the programme allows villagers living around Gunung Palung National Park to make non-cash payments for medical treatment using native tree seedlings, eco-polybags or labour for reforestation activities. The initiative also links access to affordable healthcare with forest protection, offering subsidies to communities that reduce illegal logging. Its efforts have now received international recognition, with the BBVA Foundation awarding ASRI €250,000 in its 21st Biodiversity Awards for helping restore tropical forests while improving access to healthcare.How an Indonesian clinic turned tree seedlings into medical paymentsThe initiative was established to address two interconnected problems facing communities around Gunung Palung National Park: limited access to affordable healthcare and the destruction of tropical forests.The clinic was established in 2007 by ASRI in partnership with the non-profit organisation Health In Harmony, with support from the local government. For many local families, medical emergencies could create a financial burden, while limited livelihood opportunities increased dependence on activities such as illegal logging.ASRI recognised that protecting the forest would require addressing the economic difficulties facing the communities living around it. The organisation therefore developed a healthcare model that connects medical services with environmental protection.Patients visiting its clinics can make non-cash payments for consultations and prescriptions using native tree seedlings and eco-polybags. The wider programme also accepts other forms of alternative payment, including labour for forest restoration activities.The seedlings are collected, nurtured in nurseries and eventually planted in degraded forest areas. This allows villagers to access essential medical services while directly contributing to the regeneration of their surrounding ecosystem.Villages that reduce illegal logging receive healthcare subsidiesAnother important feature of the programme is its system of healthcare subsidies linked to forest conservation.ASRI provides discounts on medical services and medicines based on the environmental practices of villages surrounding the national park. Communities that demonstrate reductions in illegal logging receive subsidised healthcare, with villages that completely stop logging qualifying for the highest level of support.The system creates a direct incentive for residents to protect their forests rather than depend on timber extraction for their livelihoods.ASRI also works with local Forest Guardians, who monitor logging activities and help assess the conservation progress of individual villages. This approach makes environmental protection a shared responsibility rather than something imposed entirely from outside.The initiative is particularly important in communities where limited employment opportunities and inadequate access to healthcare have historically contributed to pressure on forest resources.Former loggers are being encouraged to find alternative livelihoodsHealthcare payments are only one part of ASRI's wider conservation strategy. The organisation also works with people previously dependent on logging, helping them transition towards more sustainable sources of income.Its Chainsaw Buyback Programme encourages former loggers to surrender their chainsaws in exchange for financial support and assistance in developing alternative livelihoods.Participants are encouraged to explore activities such as sustainable agriculture and other forest-friendly businesses. One example is Muslianto, a former logger from Sukadana who surrendered his chainsaw and subsequently became a Forest Guardian and guide in Gunung Palung National Park.The objective is to ensure that protecting the rainforest does not come at the cost of families losing their means of earning a living.ASRI's broader approach is built around the idea that environmental conservation and community welfare cannot be addressed separately. By improving access to healthcare and supporting alternative livelihoods, the organisation aims to reduce the economic pressures that drive deforestation.Stanford study finds deforestation declined by 70%The conservation model has also reported measurable environmental results.A Stanford-led study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) in October 2020 found that deforestation in the area declined by 70% over the decade following the clinic's establishment, compared with control sites. The difference was equivalent to approximately 2,740 hectares of tropical forest.The organisation's work also supports the protection of threatened wildlife, including Bornean orangutans and Sunda pangolins, whose habitats depend on healthy forest ecosystems.According to ASRI's official programme figures, its wider conservation efforts have resulted in 701,913 tree seedlings being planted and 435 hectares of land being reforested. The organisation also reports that 343 people have handed over their logging equipment as part of its efforts to encourage alternative livelihoods.These figures reflect the organisation's cumulative programme achievements rather than results from a single year.Indonesian initiative receives €250,000 global conservation awardThe BBVA Foundation recognised ASRI in the Global category of its 21st Biodiversity Awards, announced on November 17, 2026. The organisation received €250,000 for its work restoring tropical forests in Borneo through community participation, reforestation and improved access to healthcare.The foundation also recognised two other international conservation initiatives in separate categories, each receiving €250,000.In Rwanda, the Rwanda Wildlife Conservation Association was recognised for helping revive the population of endangered Grey Crowned Cranes. Its work, involving wildlife rescue, rehabilitation, education and community monitoring, has helped increase the country's wild population from fewer than 300 birds in 2015 to 1,438 in the 2026 census.In Mexico, the Grupo de Ecología y Conservación de Islas received recognition for restoring seabird colonies across Pacific islands. Its efforts have helped recover 27 of 31 seabird colonies that had previously disappeared, benefiting at least 13 threatened species.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Historic trilateral talks: Trump, Xi and Putin meet; nuclear arms, Iran, Ukraine wars on table
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a historic trilateral meeting, with all three leaders
articles.body: US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a historic trilateral meeting, with all three leaders highlighting their countries' shared responsibility for maintaining global peace and security.Addressing the meeting, Xi said healthy interactions between major countries were not optional but a necessity. He said the three countries should work together to safeguard world peace and stability, adding that the world would descend into chaos if major powers fought.“The world is peaceful when major countries are in harmony,” Xi said, according to Chinese state media.What Xi saidXi Jinping called on the United States, China and Russia to respect each other's sovereignty, territorial integrity and core interests. He said major powers must not cross each other's "bottom lines" on sensitive issues and should respect one another to ensure peaceful coexistence.Xi also called on the three countries to encourage parties involved in ongoing conflicts to sit down for talks and resolve disputes through political means. He proposed maintaining regular high-level exchanges and establishing a crisis communication mechanism to prevent tensions from escalating.On nuclear weapons, Xi said, according to China's state news agency Xinhua, that "nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought", urging all sides to make every effort to prevent such a conflict. He also called for nuclear weapons to be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed to build a nuclear-free world.Xi further urged the three countries to abandon a Cold War mentality and avoid pursuing "decoupling and breaking chains". He said China, Russia and the US should strengthen coordination to safeguard the stability of global energy supply chains and work as partners and friends.Trump highlights trio's special responsibilityTrump described the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China as a historic moment, saying the three countries had a responsibility to maintain dialogue on issues affecting the world.“I'm delighted that this trip has also given us the opportunity for this first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia, and China. And today, in that sense, and I think in lots of other ways, we are really making history. The three of us have a great deal to discuss, and we've already discussed a lot. As presidents of three of the world's largest countries, we have a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful, and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet...” he said.Making a case for engagement despite political differences, Trump said, “Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements, and we feel the opposite, and we think that we are sure about that... Together, we are choosing a different course. A historic summit offers us the chance to seek out new opportunities and approaches on a range of very important issues. Most of them, everybody in this room knows, and hopefully to create a better future for all of us, a much better future and safer future, as the world's three largest nuclear powers by far...”On nuclear disarmament, Trump acknowledged the difficulty of persuading countries to give up their weapons.“Once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's the way life works,” he said. He also described nuclear disarmament as a difficult task, saying, “It's a very hard thing to do” to ask a leader to reduce nuclear stockpiles.Trump also called for cooperation among the three major powers, saying, “US, China & Russia must safeguard world peace, stability.” He said the countries should use dialogue to address disagreements and explore opportunities for a safer future.Putin, speaking through a translator, also said the three countries had a “joint responsibility” to maintain peace and security.Trump said the three countries were “uniquely positioned” to discuss nuclear weapons and had “special responsibilities”. He said peace could never be achieved by declining opportunities for dialogue.“Too often, past leaders avoided talking to leaders they have disagreements with,” Trump said.The historic trilateral meeting comes amid renewed focus on international arms control after the US-Russia New START treaty expired earlier this year. Washington has pushed for Beijing to join wider discussions on nuclear arms reduction, but China has traditionally resisted direct negotiations, pointing to the much larger nuclear arsenals held by the US and Russia.Before departing for Asia, Trump had said his proposed discussions with Putin and Xi would cover several major international issues, including nuclear disarmament, Iran, the Russia-Ukraine war and economic relations.“We're going to be talking about denuclearisation...We'll talk about Iran,” Trump told reporters ahead of his departure.Identifying the Russia-Ukraine war as another key subject, Trump said: “We'll also talk about my favourite subject, Ukraine. Ukraine is losing. Ukraine and Russia are losing 25,000 souls per month, so we'll be talking about that. We'll also discuss economics and trade.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A 58-year-old grandmother thought the cross she dug up in a British field after five fruitless hours was costume jewellery, but it was a medieval gold reliquary that could be worth up to £20,000
articles.summary: A British grandmother's routine day of metal detecting turned into a centuries-old discovery after she stumbled upon a small gold cross buried beneath a
articles.body: A British grandmother's routine day of metal detecting turned into a centuries-old discovery after she stumbled upon a small gold cross buried beneath a farmer's field after hours of searching. She dismissed the object as cheap costume jewelry at first, not realizing that the tiny artifact was a medieval treasure that could be worth as much as £20,000. The surprise find has since drawn attention to its historical significance and could also bring a financial reward for the hobbyist.After five hours of searching, I found something remarkableAccording to Parade and Newsbreak, the find was made in August by 58-year-old Shelley Couzins, a grandmother of five, on the Isle of Sheppey in Kent, England. Couzins, who has been into metal detecting for about four years, was out exploring a freshly plowed farmer's field with other members of the Medway History Finders group.The search began without much hope, as the grandmother is said to have found only undesirable metal objects all morning. After five hours or so of finding nothing of much value, her detector finally signaled something buried underground around lunchtime. She dug in the dirt, about 12 inches and found a small cross. The object initially looked like normal jewelry and she thought it was a costume piece rather than something of historical importance. But her understanding of the discovery changed rapidly when fellow metal-detecting enthusiasts at the group's main tent reacted. Then they realized the cross was made of solid gold. What they thought was an ordinary find was going to be a potentially valuable historical artifact.Historical importance of medieval artifactParade and Newsbreak reported that the object was quickly identified as a medieval gold reliquary cross. The artifact weighs about 10.6 grams and has two religious images on it. On one side is the crucifixion of Jesus Christ, on the other Mary holding Jesus. The find is especially significant because of its complex religious imagery and gold composition.Couzins was lucky, too, that the object survived intact. Newsbreak reported that she was relieved to find the cross undamaged, as another pass of the agricultural plow could potentially have struck and broken it. The investigating team has kept the exact location of the find secret out of fears that publicity could bring illegal treasure hunters.British Museum to assess crossWhile there's excitement about the discovery, Couzins can't just take the medieval cross home. Under Britain's treasure laws, qualifying archeological discoveries have to be reported to the relevant authorities. Having been identified and assessed the object was passed to a Finds Liaison Officer. Now the British Museum is examining the artifact and will decide if it wants to acquire it for its collection.Newsbreak says it has been valued at about £20,000 – or about $27,000. This figure is not an official valuation, however, and remains subject to the judgment of the museum.If the British Museum decides to keep the cross, an official monetary valuation will be placed on it. The money would then be split between Couzins and the land owner leaving the grandmother with a nice financial windfall.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'Heart of its nuclear program': North Korea expands Yongbyon facility as Trump seeks talks with Kim
articles.summary: North Korea has expanded its original uranium enrichment facility at its Yongbyon nuclear complex, the head of the UN nuclear watchdog has said.
articles.body: North Korea has expanded its original uranium enrichment facility at its Yongbyon nuclear complex, the head of the UN nuclear watchdog has said.The assessment by International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Grossi, cited by the Associated Press, comes as US President Donald Trump has expressed interest in meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his visit to China for the Apec forum.“Since mid-September 2026, a further extension to the original Yongbyon enrichment facility has been under construction with the new extension externally complete by late-October 2026,” Grossi said in a statement to the IAEA's board of governors on Wednesday.“The ongoing expansion of the DPRK’s (North Korea) uranium enrichment program remains a cause for serious concern,” he said, as per AP.The IAEA has not had access to Yongbyon or other sites in North Korea since Pyongyang expelled its inspectors in 2009. The agency has since relied on satellite imagery and open-source information to monitor developments in the country's nuclear programme.North Korea has described the Yongbyon complex as “the heart” of its nuclear programme. The country has facilities there to produce both highly enriched uranium and weapons-grade plutonium, two materials that can be used to build nuclear weapons.Observers say Pyongyang has taken steps to establish additional uranium enrichment facilities at Yongbyon and elsewhere since Kim's high-stakes nuclear diplomacy with Trump collapsed in 2019. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities, all of which were running daily.Trump has expressed willingness to meet Kim, but US Secretary of State Marco Rubio later said no meeting had been scheduled during the president's China visit. He added that Trump was prepared to begin a new dialogue with Pyongyang.North Korea has yet to respond to Trump's latest overture. Kim has previously said he could return to talks if Washington abandoned its “hostile policy” towards his country and recognised what he describes as North Korea's status as a nuclear state.Pyongyang wants international recognition as a nuclear-armed state, which could strengthen its demand for the lifting of UN economic sanctions.You use AI every day. articles.title: When intimacy becomes intelligence: The growing honeytrap threat to India’s armed forces.
articles.summary: To India’s Armed Forces, protecting national security is no longer just about guarding borders, securing military establishments or defending digital
articles.body: To India’s Armed Forces, protecting national security is no longer just about guarding borders, securing military establishments or defending digital networks. The threat is increasingly reaching personnel through their personal smartphones, social media accounts, private conversations and online relationships that may appear perfectly harmless. Hostile intelligence agencies and adversaries are finding ways to exploit human emotions, personal circumstances and misplaced trust to access information that would otherwise be difficult to obtain. The damage can go beyond the leakage of just classified military information. It can affect operational security, institutional confidence and the morale of the Armed Forces, most importantly.At its core, honey trapping is a well-coordinated intelligence operation that uses personal relationships to gather information and data. It is not simply about seduction or an online friendship. It involves identifying someone who has access to sensitive information, building trust with that person and gradually developing an emotional connection. Over time, that relationship can be turned into a channel for collecting sensitive information. The individual may share details without realizing that they are being targeted as part of an organized intelligence operation. In other cases, the relationship may be used for blackmail, financial pressure or gaining access to personal devices.This threat becomes more serious as India's Armed Forces become increasingly dependent on technology, as a part of the world norms. The Army, Navy and Air Force are moving towards integrated operations, advanced communications, modern surveillance systems, unmanned platforms and faster information-sharing. But behind every digital system is a person who accesses, understands and handles information. Technology can protect a server, encrypt a message or restrict access to a classified database. It cannot stop someone from discussing a military deployment in a private conversation, sharing a photograph from a sensitive location or confirming information that an adversary may already possess.This is where the human side of military security becomes important. An adversary does not always need to break into a military network if it can persuade someone with authorized access to share information. A photograph, a reference to a unit's movement, details of an upcoming exercise or even a small technical disclosure may appear harmless on its own. But when combined with satellite images, publicly available information and other intelligence inputs, these details can help an adversary understand military movements, capabilities and operational wireframes.Recent cases involving personnel of the Indian Air Force and other branches of the Armed Forces have brought this threat into sharp focus. In August 2026, a serving Indian Air Force Wing Commander was arrested by Delhi Police under the Official Secrets Act over allegations that he had shared sensitive defence information with a suspected Pakistani intelligence operative posing as a woman on social media. According to the investigation, the officer had developed an online relationship through conversations and video calls. He was allegedly persuaded to share photographs, videos and information about military deployments. He was also allegedly asked to install a data-stealing application on a colleague's mobile phone. The IAF confirmed that the officer had been under surveillance before being handed over to law enforcement agencies. Subsequent reports provided further details of the alleged information exchange. The allegations remain subject to judicial proceedings.The threat has also extended to personnel serving in other branches of the Armed Forces. In October 2026, Andhra Pradesh's Counterintelligence Cell arrested a serving sailor posted with the Eastern Naval Command. He was accused of sharing classified maritime information with a Pakistani intelligence operative through a social media honeytrap. Investigators were examining the alleged disclosure of information about naval assets, fleet movements and the Visakhapatnam naval establishment. Subsequent reports on the wider investigation referred to a suspected network involving several naval personnel and civilian associates. Investigators were looking into how ordinary-looking online profiles were used to build trust and obtain sensitive information. The investigation is ongoing, and the full extent of the alleged security breach is yet to be established.These incidents follow other cases that show how persistent the threat has become. In March 2026, the Uttar Pradesh Anti-Terrorism Squad arrested a 24-year-old Navy sailor in Agra over allegations of spying for Pakistan's ISI after he was approached through social media. In 2023, DRDO scientist Pradeep Kurulkar was arrested by Maharashtra's Anti-Terrorism Squad over allegations that he had shared sensitive defence-related information with a woman who allegedly worked for Pakistani intelligence. Earlier cases involving Air Force personnel, Army veterans and other defence-linked individuals have also shown how online relationships can be used for espionage, blackmail and financial inducement.What makes honey trapping particularly dangerous is that it rarely happens overnight. It is usually a gradual and sustained process. A person is identified and approached through what appears to be an ordinary online interaction. The conversation may begin with an interest in the individual's profession, hobbies or personal life. Over time, it can move to private messaging, phone calls, video conversations and the exchange of personal photographs. Once trust or emotional dependence develops, the person behind the profile may begin asking for seemingly harmless information. Eventually, the interaction can lead to requests for access to devices, sensitive details or, in some cases, blackmail.This raises an important question: why do educated, professionally trained and disciplined military officers fall prey to such operations? The answer is that education, rank and professional experience do not make anyone immune to emotional manipulation. Military training prepares personnel to deal with operational threats, follow procedures and work under pressure. But it does not automatically prepare every individual to recognise an intelligence operation developing through a private online relationship.In fact, an officer's professional access is often what makes that person valuable to an adversary. Military personnel may have knowledge of equipment, deployments, maintenance schedules, operational procedures, personnel movements or the functioning of sensitive establishments. An adversary does not necessarily need an officer to reveal an entire military plan. A series of small disclosures over time may be enough to confirm information, fill gaps and build a clearer picture of India's military capabilities.There are also personal circumstances that can make individuals vulnerable. Loneliness, long periods away from family, demanding postings, stress, relationship difficulties and the need for companionship can all be exploited. A carefully created online identity can offer attention, emotional support and a sense of personal connection. The individual may not initially see the interaction as a security risk. Overconfidence can also play a role. Someone who believes that their education, experience and judgement make them difficult to deceive may fail to recognise the warning signs. This does not excuse any breach of security, but it shows why counter-intelligence efforts must pay as much attention to human behaviour as they do to technology.The nature of espionage is also changing. Social media makes it easier to create convincing identities of supposed professionals, journalists, researchers, defence analysts or employees of organisations linked to the defence sector. Public photographs, professional details and social-media activity can be used to make an approach appear genuine and personal. Artificial intelligence and image-generation tools could make fake identities more convincing, while voice and video technologies may make impersonation harder to detect. However, their use in individual cases must be established through evidence. The larger concern is that online manipulation, persistent contact and digital surveillance can now work together to compromise an individual.India's military security system must therefore take the human side of the threat as seriously as cyber and physical security. A firewall can prevent unauthorised access to a network, but it cannot stop someone from voluntarily sharing information. Encryption can protect official communications, but it cannot prevent sensitive matters from being discussed through personal channels. Security systems may detect suspicious activity within a network, but they may not identify an individual being slowly manipulated outside it. Honeytrapping cannot be treated only as a cyber-security problem or a matter of individual discipline. It requires a wider response involving intelligence agencies, military leadership, personnel management, digital security and welfare across the Army, Navy and Air Force.The first step should be to make counter-intelligence awareness a regular part of military training. It should not be limited to a briefing during induction. Personnel at every rank should be taught how to identify suspicious social-media approaches, fake identities, emotional manipulation, blackmail attempts and requests for apparently harmless information. Practical exercises and realistic examples should be used to explain how such operations work. This training should cover officers, junior commissioned officers, other ranks, Agniveers, civilian defence employees and personnel serving in sensitive establishments. They must understand not only what information is classified, but also how small pieces of information can become valuable when put together.Second, the Armed Forces need stronger rules and practices for online safety. Personnel should be careful about sharing their rank, unit, location, deployment details, professional responsibilities and photographs from restricted areas. They must understand that information which appears harmless individually can become sensitive when combined with other details. Military personnel should use approved applications, enable multi-factor authentication, follow device-security rules and report suspicious links, requests for one-time passwords or attempts to install unfamiliar software. Official and personal communications should be kept separate, with strict safeguards for classified information.Third, personnel must have a safe and accessible way to report suspicious online interactions. An officer or soldier who receives an unusual approach, becomes uncomfortable with an online relationship or realises that personal information may have been compromised should be encouraged to report it immediately. Fear of embarrassment, disciplinary action or damage to one's reputation can lead people to hide such interactions until the situation becomes serious. Early reporting should be treated as a responsible security measure, not automatically as an admission of wrongdoing. At the same time, deliberate sharing of classified information must be investigated and dealt with under the law.Fourth, the Services must work more closely with counter-intelligence agencies, cybercrime investigators, intelligence units, digital platforms and financial investigators. Suspicious social-media profiles, phone numbers, payment transactions, malicious applications and connected online networks should be examined together. Investigations should not stop with the individual accused of sharing information. They must also seek to identify the people behind the operation, their intermediaries, the digital infrastructure they use and the wider networks involved. Better intelligence-sharing between the Armed Forces and civilian agencies can help identify common patterns and prevent similar incidents.Finally, personnel welfare must be recognised as an important part of national security. Regular counselling, confidential support for personal difficulties and better assistance for personnel serving away from their families can help reduce some of the vulnerabilities that hostile intelligence networks exploit. Military leadership must create an environment in which personnel can seek help without fear of being judged or embarrassed. Reporting a personal vulnerability should be seen as an act of responsibility, not weakness.For India, honeytrapping is not simply a matter of individual misconduct. It is a method through which hostile intelligence networks can use personal relationships to collect information about military deployments, infrastructure, operational capabilities and institutional processes. As the Armed Forces become more connected and dependent on technology, protecting the people who operate these systems becomes just as important as protecting the systems themselves.The security of a modern military cannot end at the firewall of a command centre or the entry gate of a military establishment. It must also extend to the individual who carries professional knowledge into the digital world. An adversary may approach through a social-media profile, a fabricated identity or what appears to be a genuine personal conversation. The larger objective may be to turn trust into access, access into information and information into a military advantage.India must therefore treat counter-honeytrapping as an essential part of military preparedness. Technology, intelligence, training, leadership and personnel welfare must work together to address this growing threat. As warfare becomes more technology-driven, the human being remains the military's greatest asset. Protecting that asset from manipulation must become an equally important part of national security.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.
